Transferred trait: Green fluorescence as a living-cell reporter
Evidence type: Direct: bacteria and whole-animal reporter expression
Biological components: gfp, encoding green fluorescent protein; single foreign reporter protein
Demonstrated result: Recombinant bacteria and nematode cells fluoresced green, establishing GFP as a reporter of gene expression and cell identity in living organisms.
Limits and caveats: Fluorescence needs external excitation light; it is not self-generated bioluminescence. The paper demonstrated reporter expression, not transfer of the jellyfish's full light-producing system.
Citation: Chalfie et al., Science (1994), Green fluorescent protein as a marker for gene expression

Demonstrated recipient(s): Tobacco Nicotiana tabacum plants and carrot Daucus carota cultured cells
Evidence type: Direct: plant cells and intact transgenic plants
Demonstrated result: Luciferase activity was detected in transformed plant-cell extracts and intact tobacco tissues. Whole transgenic plants emitted detectable light when provided luciferin.
Limits and caveats: Not autonomous: luciferin had to be supplied. Spatial light patterns reflected substrate access as well as reporter expression, so brightness was not a direct readout of expression alone.
Citation: Ow et al., Science (1986), Transient and stable expression of the firefly luciferase gene in plant cells and transgenic plants

Biological components: Four-gene set: nnluz (luciferase), nnhisps (hispidin synthase), nnh3h (hispidin-3-hydroxylase), and nncph (caffeylpyruvate hydrolase)
Demonstrated result: Engineered tobacco plants emitted self-sustained light visible to the naked eye without added luciferin, using plant caffeic-acid metabolism. Light could be imaged across growth and development.
Limits and caveats: A multienzyme pathway that depends on compatible host metabolism, not luciferase alone. Brightness varied with tissue and physiology; the result does not establish useful room illumination or universal portability to other organisms.
Citation: Mitiouchkina et al., Nature Biotechnology (2020), Plants with genetically encoded autoluminescence

Evidence type: Direct: Recipient-produced enzyme tested outside living cells
Biological components: PETase produced in the algal chloroplast.
Demonstrated result: An extracted, enriched PETase preparation changed PET and post-consumer plastic surfaces; chemical analysis detected released terephthalic acid from PET and BHET from the post-consumer material.
Limits and caveats: Not evidence that living algae assimilate PET or grow on it. The enzyme preparation was not completely pure, yields were low, and degradation was partial; post-consumer material did not yield a significant terephthalic-acid signal in the reported assay.
Citation: A PETase enzyme synthesised in the chloroplast of the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is active against post-consumer plastics (2023)

Transferred trait: Provitamin-A carotenoid synthesis in the edible endosperm
Donor organism(s): Maize (Zea mays) and Erwinia uredovora (now Pantoea ananatis)
Evidence type: Direct: Whole plants and seed biochemical measurements
Biological components: Maize phytoene synthase (PSY) plus bacterial carotene desaturase (CRTI).
Demonstrated result: Carotenoids accumulated in rice endosperm; maximum total carotenoids were 37 micrograms/g, up to 23-fold above the original Golden Rice, with preferential beta-carotene accumulation.
Limits and caveats: This paper establishes composition, not population-level prevention of vitamin A deficiency. The 37 micrograms/g figure is total carotenoids, not all beta-carotene. Host enzymes complete the pathway.

Transferred trait: Direct conversion of amorphous cellulose to ethanol
Biological components: T. reesei endoglucanase II and cellobiohydrolase II, together with A. aculeatus beta-glucosidase 1, displayed together on the yeast surface.
Demonstrated result: The three-enzyme recipient produced approximately 3 g/L ethanol from 10 g/L amorphous cellulose. The two-enzyme comparator lacking cellobiohydrolase II could not perform this direct conversion.
Limits and caveats: The demonstrated substrate was amorphous, acid-swollen cellulose, not untreated wood or highly crystalline cellulose. The result does not establish industrial economic performance.
Citation: Synergistic Saccharification, and Direct Fermentation to Ethanol, of Amorphous Cellulose by Use of an Engineered Yeast Strain Codisplaying Three Types of Cellulolytic Enzyme (2004)
